newsitem.title: UK: LPC-Future uncertain for tax-driven loans market.
newsitem.headline: LPC-Future uncertain for tax-driven loans market.

text.p: LONDON, July 3 (LPC) - The syndicated loan market is reeling from the unexpected withdrawal of tax-exempt status on preference share dividend payments, which was announced in Wednesday's UK budget, as part of Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's "Stopping Tax Leakage" package.

The ruling, which specifies that dividends on shares held by dealers, or institutions which take up preference shares with terms similar to loans, will now be taxed as trading profits, is likely to spell the end for the secretive market in tax-driven loans, which topped $10 billion last year.
"This has changed the economics of the tax loans, there is little rationale for the market now," a tax specialist said.

High-profile borrowers such as Grand Metropolitan, GECC, Disney, EDS and ToysRUs, have taken advantage of a tax loophole which has enabled them to borrow by issuing preference shares, which were repaid through tax-free dividend payments as opposed to normal taxable interest payments.

Lenders to the tax-driven deals said today that they have been advised to pull out of the transactions by tax specialists. Allowances for tax changes have been built into the documentation of the deals which allow banks to collapse the deals in five days in the event of a negative tax ruling.

Tax deals are rarely reported and have low-profile syndications - arrangers often forgo league table glory in favour of maintaining a discreet profile for their clients in order to avoid the scrutiny of the Inland Revenue Department.

Arrangers subscribe to the preference shares and take letters of credit from participating banks, while marking limits against participants in case they are unable to pay if called on due to a failure of the shares. The underlying corporate risk is often shared with participants through a guarantee structure.
The government has announced that it expects to gain 500 million stg in the period until April 2001, however banking sources estimate that the figure could be much higher.

The government's move was unexpected as the Inland Revenue had specified in June's tax bulletin that dividends on preference shares would be exempt from anti-avoidance legislation to be introduced via Schedule 7.
"The changes on the tax side have caught everyone off guard." a banking source said.

The implications of the ruling are far-ranging. The issuers are expected to bear the brunt of the fallout. Borrowers will have to buy back the preference shares and repay the banks, leaving issuers with a capital vacuum which may have to be filled by further syndicated loans - some of the deals have been structured to revert to syndicated loans in the event of a negative tax ruling.
The ruling will affect all completed deals - at least two preference share deals worth 100 million stg and $500m have been completed this year, and a Disney deal is currently in the market.

UK institutions, both clearers and merchant banks, tend to dominate as arrangers, with their UK profits and tax capacity, although Goldman Sachs is said to have acquired expertise. BZW alone arranged $5.5 billion of deals during 1996, and Lloyds is known to be an active player. Lenders are handsomely rewarded for utilising their tax positions, and the deals pay multiples of plain vanilla spreads.
The market is awaiting the submission of the finance bill to Parliament for further clarification.
